item.title: Multiple French cities announce curfew after violent weekend protests: report
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20 07:38:00
This photo taken on Oct. 17, 2026 shows a burning vehicle during a protest in Paris, France. (Xinhua/Wu Huiwo) Multiple French cities have announced curfews which will start since Monday evening after incidents of looting and violence during weekend protests, French media reported. In Paris, a curfew will be imposed from 11 p.m. Monday (2100 GMT) to 6 a.m. Tuesday (0400 GMT) around the Place de la Republique and in streets surrounding the Les Halles area, French television channel BFM TV reported, citing local authorities. In Lyon, local authorities have decided to impose a curfew from 9 p.m. Monday (1900 GMT) to 6 a.m. Tuesday (0400 GMT) in part of the Presqu'ile de Lyon, an area in the city center, BFM TV reported. The prefect of Nord department in northern France has imposed a curfew in parts of Lille, Wattignies, Douai and Denain from 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) to 6 a.m. (0400 GMT) for the next two days starting Monday, BFM TV reported, citing Matignon, the French prime minister's office. The decision was made with the agreement of all the mayors concerned. In Nice, a city in southeastern France, Mayor Eric Ciotti announced on social media platform X that a curfew for minors would take effect at 9 p.m. Monday (1900 GMT). French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said at a news conference on Monday that partial curfews would be introduced in some areas since Monday evening. Law enforcement officers stand guard outside a shop in Paris, France, Oct. 18, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Huiwo) Around 550,000 people took part in protests across France on Saturday. A total of 2,397 people were arrested during the protests marred by violence, according to figures released by the French Interior Ministry on Sunday. A total of 997 police officers and gendarmes were injured, seven of them seriously.

item.title: Chinese FM holds talks with Bulgarian counterpart
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20 07:36:00
CHINA / DIPLOMACY Chinese FM holds talks with Bulgarian counterpart By Xinhua Published: Oct 20, 2026 07:36 AM
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said here on Monday that China is ready to be Bulgaria's partner in promoting Eurasian connectivity, pursuing common development and revitalization, and practicing multilateralism. Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks during talks with Bulgarian Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova. He noted that Bulgaria is one of the first countries to recognize the People's Republic of China, and the two sides have friendly feelings toward each other. He said China-Bulgaria relations are embracing important opportunities, and his visit to Bulgaria comes at an opportune time. The two sides held in-depth discussions on planning high-level exchanges of the next stage and advancing practical cooperation in various fields, and have reached broad consensus, he added. Wang said the two sides should continuously consolidate the political foundation and strengthen communication and coordination to create important conditions for deepening mutually beneficial cooperation. China respects Bulgaria's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity, and is glad to see Bulgaria accelerate the achievement of development goals under the leadership of its new government, Wang said, adding that China is willing to be Bulgaria's long-term and reliable strategic partner in this process. He also expressed the hope that Bulgaria will continue to adhere to the one-China principle and understand and support China's legitimate position of safeguarding national sovereignty and territorial integrity. Wang said China is ready to be Bulgaria's partner in promoting Eurasian connectivity, pursuing common development and revitalization, and practicing multilateralism. The two sides should coordinate efforts to promote the joint building of the Belt and Road, the alignment with the Middle Corridor, and the cooperation between China and Central and Eastern European Countries (CEECs) and between China and the European Union (EU), so as to form a joint force and promote their respective development, he added. Wang emphasized that China and the EU are partners, not rivals, and are opportunities for each other rather than challenges. The two sides should respect and appreciate each other, pursue common achievements, and jointly shoulder international responsibilities for world peace and development, he said. China hopes the EU will work with China to uphold the correct direction of opening-up, hold high the banner of free trade, oppose unilateralism and protectionism, and find ways to handle differences and solve problems through dialogue and consultation, Wang said. Petrova said Bulgaria and China enjoy a profound traditional friendship and fruitful cooperation across various fields. Bulgaria has long adhered to and will continue firmly pursuing the one-China policy. Developing relations with China actively is a clear direction of Bulgaria's new government, she added. Bulgaria is ready to strengthen cooperation with China in such areas as economy and trade, culture and education, and to expand cooperation in high-tech and high-value-added fields, and looks forward to the early opening of direct flights between the two countries, she said. Noting that Bulgaria is located between the East and the West and serves as a crossroad connecting the Eurasian continent, Petrova said Bulgaria attaches great importance to connectivity and is willing to find more converging interests with China in this area. Bulgaria supports active dialogue between China and the EU and welcomes positive progress in China-EU trade and investment consultations, Petrova said, expressing the hope that the two sides will continue to uphold mutual respect and a pragmatic attitude, focus on the bigger picture, and find solutions that accommodate all parties' concerns. The two sides also exchanged views on the Ukraine crisis and other international and regional hotspot issues.

item.title: Japan's economic foundation undercut by defense spending
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 23:34:00
China Japan Photo: GT The Japanese government is considering a plan to increase corporate tax to fund a boost in defense spending, Japan Today reported on Sunday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The business community, however, may resist a corporate tax increase out of concern that it could hamper wage hikes and undermine Japan's international competitiveness, the report said. It wasn't long ago that the Japanese government imposed a defense surtax on companies. In March 2025, Japan introduced the 2025 Tax Reform Law and Regulations, effective April 1, 2026, which includes a 4 percent special defense surtax imposed on corporate income tax. The fact that another tax increase is being floated just months later suggests that the funding from the previous measure is already insufficient to satisfy the appetite for more defense spending - and this is happening against a backdrop of extremely fragile public finances. There is no shortage of data reflecting the fragility of the ground on which its fiscal policy stands. Japan's debt, more than twice the size of its economy, faces upward pressure due to rising social security, national defense and debt-servicing costs. Its total outstanding debt hit a record high of 1,342.17 trillion yen ($8.6 trillion) at the end of 2025, according to data from the country's Finance Ministry. Even more fundamental pressure comes from its demographic structure. Japan has the highest proportion of people age 65 and older among 39 countries with populations of at least 40 million people. The number of people age 65 and older stood at an estimated 36.24 million as of September 15, accounting for 29.6 percent of the country's total, the highest percentage on record. Such a large elderly population implies massive social security spending which, together with debt service costs, has left Japan with almost no fiscal room for maneuver. Beyond the fiscal predicament, Japan's current economy offers little cushion. According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, Japanese household spending fell 3.1 percent year-on-year in August - the ninth consecutive monthly decline. Yields on Japanese government bonds this year have climbed to multi-decade highs, while the yen has weakened to its lowest level since 1986. Wholesale prices rose 6.8 percent in the year to September, slowing from the previous month but underscoring mounting inflationary pressure that keeps alive market expectations of a near-term rate hike. The persistent downward pressure on the yen has not eased, and the high cost of imported energy and raw materials has already drastically squeezed the profit margins of a large number of manufacturers and small and medium-sized services enterprises. Against this backdrop, the Japanese government has ignored these fiscal and economic strains and kept pushing defense spending higher. The defense budget for fiscal 2026 has crossed the mark of 9 trillion yen for the first time in history, setting a new record. Japan is reportedly working to revise three key security policy documents by year-end, which would likely push annual defense outlays above 10 trillion yen. However, targeting the corporate sector for more tax revenue runs essentially counter to the government's own industrial policy goals. The corporate tax base is deeply connected to investment, employment, wage growth and industrial competitiveness, especially at a moment when Japan is trying to maintain its foothold in key sectors such as semiconductors, artificial intelligence and new energy. Japanese enterprises are already operating under high pressure. Yen depreciation has driven up import costs, labor shortages have pushed up labor expenses, and competition in the global industrial chain has grown increasingly fierce. If the corporate tax is raised further, the funds that companies had planned to use for raising salaries, investing in technological research and development, and upgrading production equipment will all be siphoned off to cover military spending. The end result will only be a further decline in corporate competitiveness, stagnant incomes for workers, and an already weak recovery in private consumption losing even more of its supporting foundation. Funding military expansion through tax hikes would squeeze Japan's financial situation and inject new uncertainty into the regional security situation. A country that keeps paying for its military buildup with tax increases will only push itself and the entire region into a far more costly confrontation. In the end, the path that erodes its own economic foundation is destined to be unsustainable.

item.title: China's Q3 economic data conveys confidence to a turbulent world: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 23:28:00
Technicians debug robots installed on the new production line at a welding workshop in Yiwu, East China's Zhejiang Province, on February 25, 2026. Photo: VCG Amid a complex and volatile external environment, China's economy has withstood headwinds and maintained steady performance, conveying confidence and certainty to a turbulent world. The stable growth of the Chinese economy provides strong safeguards for the resilience and smooth operation of global supply chains. It is injecting new momentum into the global economy and providing solid support for global demand and supply. On Monday, China's National Bureau of Statistics released the closely watched third-quarter economic data: In the first three quarters of this year, China's gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 4.6 per cent year-on-year, with growth of 4.5 per cent in the third quarter, continuing to demonstrate the resilience and vitality of the economy. Foreign media widely described the outcome as "beating estimates" or "beating expectations." Agence France-Presse (AFP) noted that the Chinese economy "is under pressure" from soaring energy costs caused by geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East. Amid such a complex and volatile external environment, China's economy has withstood headwinds and maintained steady performance, conveying confidence and certainty to a turbulent world. Amid diverging growth trends among the world's major economies and rising uncertainty, the Chinese economy - as the world's second-largest - has maintained stable performance, serving as a "ballast" for the global economy. At present, the international supply and demand system is undergoing a profound reshaping; global energy supplies remain tight, and prices for various industrial raw materials have risen sharply. In this context, in the first three quarters, the value-added output of industrial enterprises above designated size nationwide grew by 5.3 per cent year-on-year, with value-added output in high-tech manufacturing rising by 14.3 per cent, 9 percentage points faster than the growth rate for all industrial enterprises above designated size. China's industrial production remains generally stable and resilient, helping to cushion the transmission of external shocks and reduce the risk of global economic volatility. The stable growth of the Chinese economy provides strong safeguards for the resilience and smooth operation of global supply chains. As the world's manufacturing hub and a key supplier of intermediate goods, China's industrial and supply chains are deeply integrated into the global economy. The smooth operation on the production side and sustained growth in industry have ensured a stable supply of key products, components and raw materials to global markets. On the policy front, the continued promotion of high-level opening-up, the optimization of the business environment and the facilitation of trade have further consolidated China's role as a global supply chain hub. At a time when global supply chains face mounting restructuring pressures, the stable operation of the Chinese economy has effectively reduced the risks of supply chain disruptions and bottlenecks, providing a reliable guarantee for the stable production and trade activities of enterprises worldwide. Some foreign media outlets believe that the boom in artificial intelligence exports has driven the growth of China's economy. China's ever-expanding new quality productive forces have not only driven the national economy towards a development trajectory characterized by renewed momentum and an optimized structure, but are also injecting new momentum into the global economy. In the first three quarters, output of products such as 3D printing equipment, lithium-ion batteries and industrial robots maintained rapid growth, whilst new drivers such as green and low-carbon development, the digital economy and smart manufacturing continued to gain strength. These advances have not only driven the optimization and upgrading of China's domestic industrial structure but have also provided technological, product and market opportunities for the global industrial and value chains to transition towards high-end, intelligent and green development, assisting the global community in tackling climate change and promoting sustainable development. Data on China's imports and exports for the first three quarters, released by the General Administration of Customs on October 14, showed that China's imports grew by 22.3 percent, outpacing export growth. This indicates that the Chinese market continues to demonstrate a strong capacity to absorb goods from around the world. The upcoming China International Import Expo (CIIE) will attract more than 4,100 overseas companies, bringing more new products, technologies and services from across the globe to the Chinese market. China's efforts to expand opening-up are reflected not only in its products and investments going global, but also in its proactive efforts to share market opportunities with the rest of the world. Some foreign media outlets frequently focus on "trade deficits" when interpreting China's foreign trade data. Yet the figures for the first three quarters show that, as a vast, open market with a stable economy, China continues to generate orders for businesses worldwide, serving as a driving force for global trade. At present, the potential of China's domestic market still needs to be further unlocked, and the foundation for sustained economic improvement needs to be consolidated. Nevertheless, positive factors also deserve attention. In the first three quarters, the real growth of China's per capita disposable income of households was 4.4 percent, while the real growth of the per capita disposable income of rural households was 5.6 percent. Total retail sales of consumer goods and services rose by 2.6 per cent year-on-year. Search entries for the "China Haul" phenomenon keep hitting new highs. From January to August, the number of visa-free inbound foreign visitors rose 26.8% year-on-year, and tax-refund spending upon departure has surged across many regions. These trends illustrate how China's high-quality products, consumer experiences, convenient services and stable domestic demand are providing solid support for global demand and supply. China's economic report card for the first three quarters not only reflects the country's progress in high-quality development, but also provides valuable confidence and certainty for the global economy. What the world can see from these figures is that, by strengthening its supply-side foundations through innovation, enhancing growth resilience through domestic demand, and expanding opportunities for cooperation through opening-up, China's economy is transforming its current growth resilience into a long-term initiative in development, while creating more opportunities for the rest of the world.

item.title: Unitree shares surge 16.15%, market value tops 200b yuan amid China's robotics commercialization efforts
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 23:12:00
Visitors interact with a robot from Unitree Robotics during the sixth China International Consumer Products Expo (CICPE) in Haikou, south China's Hainan Province, April 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Gao Jing) Shares of Chinese robotics company Unitree Robotics surged 16.15 percent on Monday, marking their biggest single-day gain since their August 19 debut on Shanghai's STAR Market, excluding the first trading day, drawing renewed attention to the growth prospects and valuations of China's rapidly expanding embodied artificial intelligence (AI) industry. Unitree closed at 495.92 yuan per share, lifting its market capitalization back above 200 billion yuan ($28.1 billion) to 200.58 billion yuan. The stock was up as much as 19.21 percent during trading. The rally followed a steep sell-off that saw Unitree shares hit a post-listing low of 404.03 yuan on October 15, down more than 60 percent from their opening price on the first trading day, highlighting significant volatility in investor sentiment toward the sector. The rebound has also renewed debate over whether elevated valuations in China's embodied AI industry are supported by commercial progress, as robotics companies accelerate expansion while facing mounting pressure to deliver sustainable earnings. Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times on Monday that the sharp price fluctuations of the shares reflected a correction driven by short-term trading sentiment and longer-term industry expectations, rather than a fundamental shift in the sector's development prospects. Wang noted that the industry was experiencing a period of inflated valuations, with capital markets pricing in future growth potential prematurely. Investors should return to the fundamentals of industrial applications and take a rational, long-term view of the sector, he said. The industry's biggest commercialization challenge remains a mismatch between technological maturity and real-world demand, Wang said, adding that some companies' heavy reliance on related-party transactions and declining research and development intensity reflect the industry's early stage of development. Unitree remains a prominent player in China's humanoid robotics industry, despite the fluctuations. Unitree shipped more than 5,500 humanoid robots to end customers in 2025, excluding unfulfilled orders, while production exceeded 6,500 units, according to the company. However, according to figures cited in Chinese media reports, Unitree's revenue rose 48.54 percent year-on-year in the first half of 2026, while net profit excluding non-recurring gains and losses fell 19.34 percent to 244 million yuan, indicating profitability pressures despite continued revenue growth. Wang said that sustainable business models had yet to take shape across the industry, and further market consolidation and business-model adjustments would be necessary before large-scale deployment could become commercially viable. Unitree's performance comes amid broader expansion in China's robotics industry, supported by advances in artificial intelligence (AI), increasingly sophisticated manufacturing capabilities and growing demand for industrial automation. China produced 794,781 industrial robots in the first nine months of 2026, up 29.1 percent year-on-year, while service robot output reached approximately 15.59 million units, rising 7.9 percent, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Monday. China also remained the world's largest industrial robot market in 2025, accounting for 59 percent of global installations, with approximately 354,000 units installed, up 20 percent year-on-year, according to the International Federation of Robotics. China's embodied AI industry needs to shift from capital-driven expansion toward practical applications, with companies balancing technological innovation and commercialization, focusing on genuine operational needs and building sustainable growth, Wang said. China has officially approved and released its first six national standards for humanoid robots, which will take effect on April 1, 2027. The standards comprise five sets of technical requirements and a technical specification for humanoid robot simulation testing platforms. Unitree Robotics is reportedly scheduled to release its third-quarter 2026 financial results on October 29, marking its first earnings report since going public. According to a sales document previously released by the company, cumulative production of its humanoid robots (bionic bipedal models) had reached approximately 18,000 units as of July, according to media reports.

item.title: China's financial regulators roll out targeted policies at key financial forum, reaffirm opening-up
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 22:44:00
Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum (FSF) 2026 in Beijing on October 19, 2026 Photo: Ma Jingjing/GT The Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum (FSF) 2026 kicked off in Beijing on Monday, convening a heavyweight roster of top financial regulators who rolled out targeted policies, including a pilot initiative to allow overseas financial institutions to participate in yuan trading in China's interbank foreign exchange market as part of overall efforts to expand financial opening-up. Remarks by officials at the key forum reiterated China's opening-up commitments and addressed the further upgrading of opening-up toward the institutional level, experts said, adding that China's development of new quality productive forces, earnest opening-up moves, and digital and green economy will provide fresh opportunities for international investors. The People's Bank of China (PBC), the country's central bank, will roll out policies and measures, including setting up a liquidity backstop for large redemptions by non-bank financial institutions, expanding the scope of institutions eligible for the Standing Lending Facility, and rolling out a pilot initiative to allow overseas financial institutions to participate in yuan trading in China's interbank foreign exchange market, PBC Governor Pan Gongsheng said in a speech delivered at the opening ceremony of the FSF. China is firmly implementing the strategic directions and key measures set out in the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30), continuing to transform its economic growth model, expand domestic demand and advance opening-up at a high level, contributing to a new round of dynamic rebalancing in the global economy, Pan said. Zhu Hexin, deputy governor of the PBC and head of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange, said at the forum that a package of incremental measures will soon be rolled out to support enterprises in participating more effectively in international cooperation and competition, and in making better use of both domestic and international markets and resources. Zhu said that policies will be introduced to facilitate current account transactions and optimize foreign exchange management under the capital account, and efforts will be made to promote the open development of the foreign exchange market. China has always adhered to win-win cooperation and continues to promote high-level financial opening-up, with measures including actively expanding new areas for financial opening-up, supporting more foreign institutions and long-term capital to operate and invest in China, and promptly responding to the demands of foreign institutions, Ding Xiangqun, head of the National Financial Regulatory Administration, said at the opening ceremony. "The most noteworthy signal from this year's FSF lies not in another reiteration of opening-up commitments, but in the further upgrading of opening-up toward the institutional level," Tian Lihui, dean of the Institute of Financial Development at Nankai University, told the Global Times on the sidelines of the FSF on Monday. Initiatives such as strengthening financial infrastructure connectivity and supporting the offshore yuan market address not "whether foreign capital can enter," but "whether it can stay after entry." The joint appearance of major financial regulators and the parallel emphasis on opening-up and risk control also constitute a form of expectation management, and institutional opening-up is controllable and predictable, Tian said. The new reform and opening-up measures came after China issued a plan in September to strengthen its financial sector during the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period. According to the plan, China aims to put in place the overall framework of a modern financial system with Chinese characteristics by 2030, while largely establishing a highly adaptive, competitive, and inclusive modern financial system with Chinese characteristics by 2035. As China's macro policies gain traction and innovation momentum continues to build, the underlying conditions and fundamental trend of China's economy moving toward higher quality and long-term soundness remain strong, Wu Qing, chairperson of the China Securities Regulatory Commission, said at the ceremony. The underlying logic of the capital market's operation has undergone profound shifts, making the allocation value of Chinese assets even more compelling, he said. Under the theme of "Building an Open Collaborative and Inclusive Ecosystem for Global Financial Development," the Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum 2026 is taking place in Beijing from Monday to Thursday. This year, the event attracted the participation of more than 400 prominent guests from more than 40 countries and regions. This year's event features discussions on economic governance, financial innovation, artificial intelligence (AI), capital market development, cross-border financial cooperation and global financial governance, according to the official agenda. It also includes a China-EU Financial Investment Forum, and sessions focusing on financial support for the real economy, technological innovation and private sector development. A stroll through Beijing's Xicheng district reveals Financial Street in full forum mode. Blooming floral displays line the boulevard from end to end, while FSF logos and banners punctuate everything from street corners to lamp posts. Launched in 2012 to mark two decades of the area's development, the FSF has since grown into a flagship platform that not only raises the district's international profile but also cements its place on the global financial map. The FSF has become an important window for the international community to observe China's financial reform and opening-up. A key message from this year's forum is that China remains committed to financial opening-up, with a growing focus on aligning its rules and institutions with international standards, Hu Qimu, professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times on Monday. "China is shifting from an emphasis on market access toward institutional opening-up, including improving regulation, enhancing transparency and facilitating cross-border investment," said Hu, noting that amid global economic uncertainty, these efforts will help stabilize market expectations and strengthen international investors' confidence in China's long-term prospects. Moreover, China's appeal to international capital lies in its vast market, comprehensive industrial system and ongoing economic transformation, said Hu. The expert added that emerging sectors such as AI, new energy, advanced manufacturing and the digital economy offer substantial investment opportunities, supported by the country's strong industrial supply chains and innovation capabilities.

item.title: US-Japan drills lay bare true meaning of Japan's 'exclusive defense' narrative
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 20:45:00
Representatives of groups opposing the upcoming Japan-US joint military exercise Keen Sword 27, along with prefectural assembly members, submit a petition addressed to Oita Governor Sato on October 15, 2026 at the prefectural government office, calling for the cancellation of the exercise scheduled to begin on October 19, 2026. Photo: Screenshot of Oita Asahi Broadcasting If a force repeatedly insists that it is acting in self-defense, perhaps the best way to judge is not its press releases, but where it places its missiles. According to Japanese media, US-Japan Keen Sword 27 military exercises - "seen as a dress rehearsal for defending Japan's southwestern island chain" - kicked off Monday. This year's exercise is the largest of its kind to date. But what is this "sword" really for? The answer is not in the exercise's introduction, but in a string of firsts. The first "first": The drill will see Japan for the first time deploy its longer-range Type 25 surface-to-ship missiles outside their base in Kumamoto Prefecture. It derived from the Type 12 anti-ship missile. As its name may have maintained understated, its reported range has surged from roughly 200 kilometers to 1,000 kilometers. Reports say the range puts much of the East China Sea, parts of China's coast and the Korean Peninsula within reach. This is no longer simply a defensive system. With its extended range, it substantially increases Japan's ability to conduct long-range strikes. Deploying it in a major exercise is a clear indication that Japan's military is expanding. The second "first": The US' NMESIS anti-ship missile system will be deployed to Yonaguni Island, barely 110 km from Taiwan island, for the first time. Though marketed as an anti-ship system, NMESIS can fire cruise missile Naval Strike Missile, which provides precision land-attack capabilities. It means a once-quiet maritime outpost is being turned into a forward military position capable of launching strikes The third "first": Five countries - France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines - will join the exercise for the first time. The drills let Washington show it can still rally partners in the Western Pacific, while giving Tokyo a chance to wrap its expanding military role - and its move away from exclusive defense - in the appearance of allied consent. The fourth "first": The exercise is expanding further into emerging domains of warfare. Alongside traditional drills involving integrated air and missile defense and ground operations training, the exercise also includes cyberattack response, information warfare training and electromagnetic warfare training. It signals Japan's drive to enhance its abilities in emerging domains of warfare and deepen the "modernization" of the US-Japan alliance. Nevertheless, a country committed to exclusively defense-oriented policy has little reason to rehearse 1,000-kilometer missiles strikes, or to station offensive-capable weapons on small islands sitting right next to its neighbors. These steps indicate that the US and Japan are moving past conventional island defense, converting Japan's southwestern islands into forward nodes for projecting power outward. The region is concerned not simply because the exercise is larger, but because Japan's placement of weapons is changing what "defense" means in practice. Japan's ambitions pose longer-term risks. It seems to be using joint drills to steadily erode the limits of exclusive defense, after all, 1,000-km missiles far exceed any narrow territorial requirement. At the same time, it is trying to integrate more deeply into US operations, moving from a protected ally toward a core role in the forward posture along the First Island Chain. These efforts also align with Tokyo's wider push to revise the pacifist constitution. Taken together, they raise serious questions about where Japan's postwar security identity is heading. European participants are largely symbolic. They may be willing to appear in an exercise, but that does not mean they are prepared to bear the heavy costs of a conflict in the Western Pacific. The US, for its part, has long kept strategic ambiguity on Taiwan question. Whether Washington would fight on Japan's behalf in a crisis remains an entirely different question. As for Japan, Tokyo seems to think that tightening its alignment with Washington and acquiring offensive-capable weapons will boost its geopolitical position. Yet this overlooks a stark reality: Stationing missiles only 110 kilometers from Taiwan island would place Japan on the front line of one of the region's most volatile flashpoints if fighting broke out. Waving weapons on one's own doorstep can hardly bring lasting peace. More often, it simply stacks the risks higher and puts one closer to the flames. Japan once pursued a militarist path that brought great suffering to Asia. As it now boosts its military role again, the question is not just how much protection it says it needs, but how it will prove it will not repeat that history. When Japan's missile ranges run ahead of peace commitments, and long-range strike power quietly supplants exclusive defense, the more prominently Keen Sword is displayed, the heavier the shadow it may cast across the region.

item.title: Chinese actress cancels Bangkok fan meeting amid embassy travel safety alert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 19:15:00
Bai Lu Photo: IC Chinese actress Bai Lu on Monday canceled her fan meeting in Bangkok scheduled for Sunday, citing risk warnings following recent alleged missing, scam incidents in Thailand, and pledged to compensate eligible fans for related flight and hotel cancellation or change fees. According to a statement released by Bai’s official studio on Sina Weibo, the Meet & Love Bai Lu Special Fan Meeting, scheduled for October 25 in Bangkok, had been canceled following consultations with the platform amid recent risk warnings. Bai, whose original name is Bai Mengyan, is a Chinese actress and model born in 1994 and best known for her roles in TV series such as Untouchable Lovers , One and Only and Forever and Ever . The statement said that the fan meeting was canceled after careful assessment, with the safety of attendees and trouble-free travel arrangements identified as the studio’s and organizers’ top priorities. The statement also said that Bai and her studio offered to compensate eligible domestic and overseas fans who purchased tickets through official channels for actual flight and hotel cancellation or change fees related to the canceled Bangkok event, covering travel from October 24 to 26. The Chinese Embassy in Thailand warned last Friday that there had recently been several cases of Chinese nationals going missing, being illegally detained or being deceived into traveling onward to the Thai-Myanmar border after entering Thailand. The embassy said criminals had lured Chinese nationals to Thailand under the pretext of high-paying jobs, business visits, investment opportunities and project invitations, then subjected them to criminal acts, threatening their personal safety and property. It also warned of recent scams targeting livestreamers and performers in China with fraudulent invitations to filming and performance engagements. The Chinese Embassy in Thailand urged Chinese nationals visiting the country to stay alert to scams and take precautions to ensure their safety. Global Times

item.title: Chinese scientists trace local origins of early millet farmers in northern China
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 18:52:00
Photo: Courtesy of Huang Chinese scientists have found genetic evidence that early millet-farming populations in northern China originated locally rather than emerging from a major influx of migrant agricultural groups, according to research published in the journal Science Advances. The research analyzed genome-wide data from seven ancient individuals at the Donghulin site in Beijing and the Dengcaogouliang and Sitai sites in Zhangjiakou, North China's Hebei Province, combined with carbon-14 dating and stable isotope evidence. It covers a period from about 11,000 to 7,300 years ago. The study was conducted by teams led by Huang Yanyi and Pang Yuhong of Peking University's Biomedical Pioneering Innovation Center, together with Zhao Chaohong and Wu Xiaohong from the university's School of Archaeology and Museology, and collaborating archaeological institutions. Huang told the Global Times that the research employed multidisciplinary and hi-tech methods. Combining ancient genomics, archaeological remains and dietary evidence, it has revealed the genetic continuity and local origin of millet-related populations in the region. According to Huang, the origins of the earliest populations that used and cultivated millet, and whether the intensification of millet farming was driven mainly by local people or by incoming farming groups, had long been difficult to resolve because of a lack of direct genetic evidence from early millet-related populations. Zhao Chaohong, one of the research fellows, told the Global Times that because the Donghulin site is older than other sites and has yielded more material, the research team began work there first. "New discoveries during later excavations at the Dengcaogouliang and Sitai sites brought human and plant remains into the same research framework, ultimately shaping this multidisciplinary collaboration," said Zhao. Zhao explained that the excavations had uncovered a relatively large number of individuals, but the study selected representative individuals whose stratigraphic context and dating data were relatively clear. Three were from the Donghulin site, with individuals from the other two sites also included, for a total of seven. "We selected these individuals to examine kinship and, together with agricultural remains, to see whether early agriculture was domesticated by these people," Zhao said. He added that continuous chronological material from Donghulin and other sites allows research fellows to observe when agriculture began to emerge in northern China and how it persisted afterward. The study found that three ancient individuals from the Donghulin site were genetically close to one another and had relatively close genetic ties to contemporaneous hunter-gatherer populations in the Heilongjiang River basin. The findings point to deep ancestral links among early Holocene populations in inland northern East Asia. Further comparison showed that the populations at the Dengcaogouliang and Sitai sites were, genetically speaking, highly similar to the Donghulin population, belonging to the same northern inland genetic branch of East Asia. The Dengcaogouliang people retained ancestry most closely related to Donghulin, with no significant mixture from outside groups, suggesting that the local genetic background persisted for more than 3,000 years. At the same time, dietary evidence indicated a clear shift. Combined with archaeological evidence, the research fellows found that C4 crops, plants that use the C4 carbon fixation pathway to concentrate carbon dioxide around the enzyme Rubisco, including millet, became increasingly important in the diet of the studied populations. The continuity in genetic background alongside the dietary shift supports the view that millet farming in the region developed mainly on the basis of local populations, providing genetic support for the local origin of early millet-farming groups. The study also found that Donghulin-related ancestry contributed to the formation of early hunter-gatherer populations around Lake Baikal and in Mongolia. "The study shows the interaction between inland northern populations and neighboring groups and their influence on later populations, offering new evidence for understanding the relationship between the development of millet farming and the population history in East Asia," said Huang.

item.title: China's Central Archives opens over 5,000 Long March items to mark 90th anniversary
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19 10:10:00
China's Central Archives opens more than 5,000 Long March-related archival items to the public on October 19, 2026 to mark the 90th anniversary of the Red Army's Long March victory. Photo: CCTV News China's Central Archives opened more than 5,000 Long March-related archival items to the public on Monday to mark the 90th anniversary of the Red Army's Long March victory, offering firsthand accounts of key battles, strategic decisions and solidarity between soldiers and civilians, according to state broadcaster CCTV News. The newly accessible materials mainly date from October 1934 to October 1936, including programs and declarations issued by the Communist Party of China (CPC), Red Army telegrams and reports on operational deployments, and revolutionary newspapers and periodicals founded and published by the CPC. Together, they showcase the revolutionary spirit of the CPC and the people's armed forces, vividly depicting how the Red Army and ordinary people stood united, braved sacrifice and pressed ahead during the Long March, according to CCTV News. Among the materials opened to the public for the first time is Jiebao (victory bulletin), a newspaper founded by the CPC's Shanghai central bureau. A total of 40 issues were published between October 1933 and June 1935, exposing the reactionary rule of the Kuomintang, publicizing the Red Army's military achievements and development in the revolutionary base areas. Liu Kun, a staff member of the Central Archives' archival access department, was cited as saying that "the issue of Jiebao , published on December 17, 1934, carried a report stating, 'The westward-bound Red Army has victoriously captured Liping in Guizhou' … Liping was the site of the first Political Bureau meeting held by the CPC Central Committee after the Long March had begun. The Liping Meeting affirmed the decision to change course at Tongdao and established the Red Army's strategy of advancing westward, thereby averting the risk of being encircled and annihilated by Kuomintang forces had it continued north." The words "utmost urgency" on the telegram testify to the critical military situation at the time. The words "utmost urgency" on the telegram testify to the critical military situation at the time. Another document, titled "Report on the first division's covering of the entire army's bridge crossing tomorrow," provides a detailed account of the Red Army's exploits in capturing Luding Bridge, said Liu. "The capture of Luding Bridge was one of the major victories of strategic significance during the Red Army's Long March," Liu said. "As a firsthand battlefield record, this document details when units of the First Red Army Corps arrived at Luding Bridge and launched their attacks. It also records the situation on the ground as they captured the bridge, defeated a regiment of Sichuan troops and seized military supplies. The document states, 'Today, we captured more than 100 prisoners and over 100 firearms, along with enough ammunition and hand grenades to substantially replenish our supplies.'" The 25th Red Army set out from Hejiachong in Luoshan county, Henan Province, on November 16, 1934, and arrived in Yongping, Shaanxi Province, on September 15, 1935, to become the first Red Army force to reach northern Shaanxi during the Long March. A special report submitted to the CPC Central Committee on July 17, 1935, by Wu Huanxian, the political commissar of the 25th Red Army, is an important historical source for research into the force's Long March. "In this report, Wu perceptively raised the question of whether they could join forces with the 26th and 28th armies, concentrate their strength to destroy enemy forces, support the main Red Army's operations in the northwest, and swiftly establish a new, strong and consolidated revolutionary base there," Liu said. "Operating in isolation, without instructions from the CPC Central Committee or deployments ordered by higher authorities, the CPC Hubei-Henan-Shaanxi Provincial Committee resolutely decided that the main force of the 25th Red Army should advance westward and northward to support the main Red Army. Wu's report also explains the thinking behind that decision," Liu said. Starting Monday, audiences can consult these materials at the Central Archives' public reading hall by presenting valid identification, such as a national ID card or work ID, per CCTV News.
